data.title: Malé Kozmálovce – the Grác guard hillfort in the Slovak Gate
data.excerpt: The Grác hillfort above Malé Kozmálovce belongs to the chain of guard hillforts in the Slovak Gate, whose task was to protect the entrance to the Hron region. A rampart encloses an irregular quadrangle of 2.4 ha, and in 1938 the grave of a Slavic warrior with a Carolingian sword of type X was found north of the village.
data.metaTitle: Malé Kozmálovce – the Grác guard hillfort
data.metaDescription: The Grác guard hillfort near Malé Kozmálovce protected the entrance to the Hron region through the Slovak Gate, above all after Great Moravia broke apart.

children.text: The Grác – Malé Kozmálovce hillfort lies about 4 km north-west of Starý Tekov. It belongs to the guard hillforts of the Slovak Gate area, whose task was to protect the entrance to the Hron region. The importance of the hillfort, together with the other guard hillforts built in the

, grew above all in the period after central Great Moravian authority broke apart at the beginning of the 10th century, when they protected the local Slavic population against attacks by the Old Hungarians.

In 1938, during deep trenching in a vineyard north of the village, the grave of a Slavic warrior was found. Beside the skeleton lay a Carolingian sword of type X, two iron stirrups and a pot decorated with a wavy line. The grave can be dated to the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century.

Three further graves, said to have contained clay vessels and iron spears (only one barrel-shaped vessel has survived from the finds), were identified in 1947 while sand was being dug on a rise north of the village, between the road to Tlmače and a vineyard. Unfortunately these finds were not recovered by specialists and more detailed information about the circumstances of their discovery is lacking.

The remains of the earthwork defences, that is of the hillfort, have survived on the eastern part of the hill of Pipíška, known as Grác, which is covered with an acacia wood and, in its southern part, with vineyards. The eastern edge of the hill falls steeply away in a rocky scarp into the floodplain of the Hron, which forms a natural defence of the site. On the remaining sides the site was protected by a rampart, which joined the said rocky scarp with its eastern ends and enclosed an area in the shape of an irregular quadrangle with rounded corners (2.4 ha). On the better-preserved stretches the rampart stands 3 m above the ground on the outside and 2 m on the inside of the hillfort. The material for its mound was partly obtained on the spot, but no pronounced ditch can be made out along the rampart. A large part of the fortification was built of stone, which is not bonded with mortar. The area enclosed in this way is divided by a low rampart running south–north into two parts, a western and an eastern one. On the basis of surface finds of pottery, both the occupation of the site and its fortification can be dated to the 9th or 10th century.
